channel.description: daily selected and enriched macroeconomic and political news

item.title: The Conference Board's US consumer confidence index rose 11.4 points to 103.3 in November, its second consecutive rise and its highest level since January 2025, after falling in September to its lowest since April 2014.
item.description:
The Present Situation Index rose 13.7 points to 132.8 and the Expectations Index, which tracks households' six-month outlook for income, business and employment, rose 9.9 points to 83.6, Anadolu Agency reports. The share of respondents saying jobs were plentiful rose to 30.8% from 26.2%, while the share saying jobs were hard to get fell to 18.4% from 21.4%, and the share expecting fewer jobs in the coming months fell to 19.3% from 25.7%. BNN Bloomberg reports that the improvement could signal a pickup in consumer spending, but that economists say the surveys are less reliable measures of consumer behaviour than they were in the past. The reports do not give spending or retail sales data.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

US households' confidence has recovered sharply in two months from a multi-year low. On a general reading rather than on anything in the sources, confidence indicators often move ahead of spending, but the link is weaker than in the past on the economists' account, so measured spending data are the stronger test. On the same general reading, for adhesive technologies, higher consumer spending would support demand for consumer goods, cars and home improvement. Points that may be worth considering include whether holiday-season retail sales confirm the rise, and whether the jobs readings are confirmed by employment data.

Anadolu Agency | BNN Bloomberg

item.title: A Saudi-led coalition has launched an airstrike on Yemen's Hodeidah port after an evacuation warning, The Times of India reports; the Houthis had said they would target all Saudi Red Sea ports, including Jeddah, if Hodeidah was attacked.
item.description:
The strike followed a call by coalition spokesperson Major General Turki al-Maliki for civilians to leave designated areas of the port. In a separate development, an attack on Riyadh's Financial Centre injured eleven people, The Times of India reports; the summary does not say who carried it out. The UK has imposed sanctions on the Houthi group, including an asset freeze, and on four of its officials, and is providing defensive military support to Saudi Arabia, including air defence, aerial refuelling and Typhoon fighter jets, UK Middle East minister Stephen Doughty said, Arab News reports. The UK government gave as reasons the Houthis' escalation of fighting inside Yemen, attacks on civilian infrastructure in Saudi Arabia and disruption of shipping in the Red Sea and the Bab al-Mandeb Strait. The reports do not give the damage at Hodeidah, the date of the strike, or any effect yet on shipping.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

The conflict between the Saudi-led coalition and the Houthis now involves a strike on a Yemeni Red Sea port and a Houthi threat against Saudi Red Sea ports, including Jeddah. On a general reading rather than on anything in the sources, attacks on Saudi Red Sea ports such as Jeddah would add risk to a shipping route that links Asia and Europe through the Suez Canal. On the same general reading, for adhesive technologies, renewed disruption in the Red Sea would affect freight costs and lead times for chemical raw materials and finished goods moving between Asia, the Middle East and Europe. Points that may be worth considering include whether the Houthis carry out their threat against Saudi ports, and whether shipping companies change routes or insurance terms for the Red Sea.

The Times of India | Arab News

item.title: China's commerce ministry has extended its suspension of restrictions on exports of gallium, germanium, antimony and superhard materials to the United States until 27 January 2027.
item.description:
The Ministry of Commerce announced on 24 November that the suspension, which covers strategic materials, will now run from 28 November 2026 to 27 January 2027, Commercial Times reports. The extension prevents the restrictions from coming back into force and gives US semiconductor and high-tech industries more time to obtain these raw materials. Gallium and germanium are used in semiconductors, optoelectronics and communications, and antimony in flame-retardant materials, batteries and other industrial uses. The News International reports that the move aims to prevent escalation in the trade truce after the summit between Xi Jinping and Donald Trump. The reports do not say whether exports still need licences, or what volumes are involved.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

The extension removes the risk that these export restrictions on materials for semiconductors and flame retardants would return at the end of November, but only for two months. On a general reading rather than on anything in the sources, a short extension keeps supply available but leaves buyers planning around a new date, which tends to keep inventories and prices high. On the same general reading, for adhesive technologies, antimony compounds are used with flame-retardant formulations, and gallium and germanium matter for the semiconductor customers of electronics materials, so the supply risk is moved rather than removed. Points that may be worth considering include whether the suspension is extended again before 27 January, and whether the restrictions apply to supplies routed through other countries.

Commercial Times | The News International

item.title: The US Trade Representative is expected to publish findings of a Section 301 probe into industrial overcapacity in 16 economies, including China and the EU, as soon as this week and to propose tariffs on most of their products, sources say.
item.description:
According to Business Day, citing three people familiar with the matter, the investigation covers China, the EU, India, Japan, South Korea, Mexico, Vietnam, Taiwan, Thailand, Malaysia, Indonesia, Switzerland, Norway, Singapore, Bangladesh and Cambodia. The new duties would partly replace global import tariffs struck down by the US Supreme Court in February, and steel, aluminium and cars, already covered by national-security tariffs, may be excluded. POLITICO, citing a person with knowledge of the planning, reports that the proposed duties will honour negotiated ceilings, so China's overall tariff rate would not exceed 20% and the EU's would stay below its 15% cap, and that countries can respond through hearings, public comments and talks before rates are final. Handelsblatt reports that the investigation also partly targets Chinese investment in Southeast Asia, to prevent tariffs being circumvented. The timing could still change. European stock markets fell on 24 November on the tariff reports, with Frankfurt down 1.04%, Il Sole 24 Ore reports, and on 25 November MSCI's broadest index of Asia-Pacific shares outside Japan was down 2.3% as tariff fears returned and a tech-led rally faded, The Straits Times reports. The reports do not give final tariff rates or product lists.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

This would be a broad new layer of US tariffs on most goods from the largest trading partners, within ceilings already negotiated, rather than a single-product measure. On a general reading rather than on anything in the sources, a proposal followed by hearings and comments leaves time for rates and exclusions to change, and the ceilings limit the increase for partners with trade deals, while economies without such caps carry more uncertainty. On the same general reading, for adhesive technologies, tariffs on most products would reach both imported materials and finished goods that contain bonded components, so the product scope and any exclusions matter more than the headline rate. Points that may be worth considering include which product groups the proposal lists, how rates compare with the negotiated caps, and how the US–China trade truce reached in Busan is handled, which Chinatimes reports is set to expire on 10 January and which experts say can be extended if added tariffs stay within the agreed limits.

Commercial Times | Business Day | POLITICO | Il Sole 24 Ore | Handelsblatt | Chinatimes | Il Sole 24 Ore | The Straits Times

item.title: Thailand's car production fell 35.19% year on year in October to 87,938 vehicles, after a 6.08% fall in September, and exports also fell sharply, largely because of flood disruption, while domestic sales rose 8.71%, the Federation of Thai Industries says.
item.description:
According to the Federation of Thai Industries, reported by Business Recorder, car exports fell sharply in October, largely because of disruption from recent flooding, despite higher domestic sales. Domestic car sales rose 8.71% year on year in October after a 14.28% rise in September, which the spokesperson of the federation's automotive industry club, Surapong Paisitpattanapong, attributed to purchases of electric vehicles. The summary does not give the export volume, which plants were affected by the floods, or when production is expected to recover.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

Thailand's car output fell by more than a third in October while domestic sales grew. On a general reading rather than on anything in the source, an export fall caused by flood disruption is likely to be temporary once plants and logistics recover, unlike a fall in demand, but it can disrupt supply to export markets in the meantime. On the same general reading, for adhesive technologies, lower car output in Thailand reduces demand for automotive bonding and sealing materials there for as long as it lasts, while rising domestic electric vehicle sales point to a changing product mix. Points that may be worth considering include how quickly exports recover in November and December, and whether production of electric vehicles in Thailand grows with domestic sales.

Business Recorder

item.title: US industrial leasing tied to data-centre development and operations reached 50 million square feet in January–September 2026, 113% above the full-year 2025 total, far outpacing a 21% rise in total new industrial leasing, Cushman & Wakefield says.
item.description:
According to Cushman & Wakefield's report, as reported by MarketScreener, data-centre-related users accounted for 25% of US leases of over 1 million square feet signed in 2026 and 11% of all new leasing so far this year, reaching a record 14% in the third quarter. The supply chain around data centres is expanding: more than 47 gigawatts of data-centre capacity is operational in the US and another 36 gigawatts is under construction. US imports of AI-related equipment, parts and components rose 62% from a year earlier to USD 659 billion so far this year. The summary does not say over which period the 21% rise in total new industrial leasing is measured, which activities the leased space is used for, or how much construction spending it represents.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

Data-centre demand now accounts for a record share of US industrial leasing. On a general reading rather than on anything in the source, leased industrial space for data-centre supply chains is used for storing and assembling equipment such as servers, power and cooling systems, which links the data-centre build-out to manufacturing and logistics activity beyond the data-centre sites themselves. On the same general reading, for adhesive technologies, data centres draw on bonding, sealing and thermal management materials in electronics, power equipment and building envelopes, so 36 gigawatts under construction points to continued demand in these applications. Points that may be worth considering include how much of this demand depends on continued AI investment, how quickly capacity under construction comes into operation, and whether the share of data-centre users in industrial leasing keeps rising in the fourth quarter.

MarketScreener

item.title: The European Commission has set provisional safeguard quotas on hybrid passenger car imports from all origins for up to 200 days from 1 December, under which China may ship just over 190,000 hybrids to the EU until mid-June 2027.
item.description:
The implementing regulation of 23 November was published in the EU Official Journal on 24 November, Dünya reports. The measures cover full hybrids and plug-in hybrids, according to MarketScreener. The Commission cited a sharp increase in imports and an imminent threat of serious injury to EU manufacturers, Anadolu Agency reports, and set country quotas for every country with more than 2% of EU hybrid imports in 2025 plus a residual quota for all others. ABC.es lists quotas for Japan, Turkey, the UK, South Korea, Mexico, Morocco and the US, among others, until 18 June 2027; the measures can become definitive nine months after the investigation started. Turkey's quota for 1 December to 28 February is 56,844 vehicles; unused quota carries over, and imports above it are stopped rather than charged extra duty, according to Dünya. Asharq Al-Awsat reports that the quota for major exporters was set at just over 15% above their 2025 import levels, and that it follows an October agreement with China. The EU opened its investigation on 30 October. China's commerce ministry said it would resolutely safeguard Chinese industries' interests and that it hopes the EU will abide by the agreed arrangement, WTO rules and the principle of non-discrimination. The reporting does not give total quota volumes for all countries or expected price effects.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

This is a provisional but binding trade measure on the EU car market: quotas per country with a hard stop, not a tariff that importers can pay. On a general reading rather than on anything in the sources, a cap on imported hybrids leaves EU demand for hybrids to be met more from cars built in the EU or from producers that build there, which may move some production into Europe over time. China Daily writes that the EU reportedly plans to limit Chinese imports in sectors including furniture, chemicals and machinery, with tariffs on volumes above quota, possibly as early as the first quarter of 2027; that is China Daily's account and is not confirmed in the other sources. On the same general reading, for adhesive technologies, any shift of hybrid assembly into the EU would change where automotive bonding and sealing materials are needed, and a quota approach extended to chemicals would affect material sourcing. Points that may be worth considering include how quickly the quotas fill, whether China responds with measures of its own, and whether the quota approach is used in other sectors.

Dünya | Anadolu Agency | ABC.es | MarketScreener | Asharq Al-Awsat | Xinhua | China Daily

item.title: Taiwan's industrial production index rose 29.8% year on year in October, its strongest single month in 16 years, as computer, electronic and optical products output grew 1.3-fold on stronger export orders and server makers' product mix, the ministry says.
item.description:
Taiwan's Ministry of Economic Affairs says the manufacturing production index rose 31.63% to 154.61 in October, its 32nd consecutive month of growth, Commercial Times reports. Output in computers, electronic and optical products rose 1.3-fold year on year on stronger export orders and server makers' product mix, and electronic components grew 25% on AI demand, according to Chinatimes. In January–October, industrial production rose 21.52% and manufacturing 22.88%. The ministry's Department of Statistics expects the manufacturing index to rise 22.2% to 26% year on year in November. Separately, the output value of Taiwan's display industry is projected to fall 2.9% to about TWD 760.3 billion in 2026, as rising memory prices raise the cost of consumer electronics and reduce their shipments, according to Chang Hung-Yi, an analyst at ITRI's Industrial Economics and Knowledge Center, Commercial Times reports. The reports do not give production volumes outside electronics.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

Taiwan's industrial output grew at its fastest single-month pace in 16 years in October, driven by servers and electronic components, while the display panel industry is under pressure from memory costs that weigh on consumer electronics. On a general reading rather than on anything in the sources, Taiwan's production is a leading indicator for the global electronics supply chain, because a large share of AI servers and components is made or assembled there. On the same general reading, for adhesive technologies, electronics assembly uses bonding, encapsulation and thermal materials, so demand from AI servers and components is strong while demand from consumer devices may weaken. Points that may be worth considering include whether the November reading meets the ministry's range, and how far higher memory prices reduce consumer electronics output in 2027.

Commercial Times | Chinatimes | Commercial Times

item.title: Germany's Ifo business climate index rose to 90.6 in November from a revised 90.1 in October, slightly above the 90.5 analysts expected, but it fell in manufacturing and construction while rising in services and trade.
item.description:
Companies were more satisfied with their current business and raised their expectations, MarketScreener reports. The overall figure was just above the consensus of 90.5 in a Reuters poll of analysts. The index rose in services and trade; in manufacturing and construction, it fell. The summary does not give the index levels for each sector, the separate figures for current conditions and expectations, or the reasons companies gave.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

The headline improvement in German sentiment does not extend to manufacturing and construction. On a general reading rather than on anything in the source, a business climate index measures how companies judge their situation and outlook, not output or orders, so a fall in manufacturing and construction is an early indication rather than a measured change in demand. On the same general reading, for adhesive technologies, manufacturing and construction are the main German customer sectors, so their weaker sentiment matters more for demand than the overall rise, with services and trade improving. Points that may be worth considering include whether the manufacturing and construction readings are confirmed by orders and output data, and whether the gap between services and industry widens in December.

MarketScreener

item.title: EU new-car registrations rose 5.4% to just under 9.46 million in January–October, ACEA data show, and battery-electric cars took 23.4% of them against 16.4% a year earlier, while petrol and diesel registrations fell by about a fifth.
item.description:
Figures from the European Automobile Manufacturers' Association (ACEA), reported by MarketScreener, show about 2.21 million battery-electric cars registered in the EU in the first ten months. In October alone, EU registrations across all powertrains rose 2.6% to 939,447. Le Parisien reports that non-rechargeable hybrids remain the largest group, with 36% of ten-month registrations (3.4 million), against 20.8% for petrol and 6.9% for diesel, and that electric car sales grew 79.4% in France and 60.7% in Germany over the ten months. Chinese brands gained ground: across Europe, Lianhe Zaobao reports, registrations of six large Chinese carmakers rose 71.3% in October to 167,259, lifting their share to 14.8% from 9%, within a European market up 3.4% to about 1.13 million. In the EU, Volkswagen-group brands edged down to 2.47 million over ten months while BYD rose more than 150% to 237,137, and in October Renault and Volkswagen fell 8.5% and 9%. The reporting does not give production volumes in Europe, how many of the hybrids were imported, or prices.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

Car volumes in the EU are growing modestly, while the powertrain mix is moving quickly and Chinese brands are gaining share in Europe, and the EU's new hybrid import quotas (see other insight in this alert) take effect in this market. On a general reading rather than on anything in the sources, a car's bill of materials changes more with its powertrain than with the total count of cars, because battery-electric cars carry battery packs, thermal management systems and body structures that are assembled differently from combustion cars. On the same general reading, for adhesive technologies, a fast-rising battery-electric share points to more battery bonding, thermal interface and structural bonding per car, and a rising share of Chinese brands may shift where those materials are specified and qualified. Points that may be worth considering include whether battery-electric growth holds in markets where incentives change, how much of the Chinese brands' volume is produced in Europe, and how established European brands' falling registrations show up in their production plans.

MarketScreener | Le Parisien | Lianhe Zaobao | MarketScreener
